a_raw: {"translation":"Target is the following proposition: For every set K of arithmetic sentences and every arithmetic theory F, assume that the axiom set F is recursively enumerable and that every theorem of IΣ₁ is a theorem of F (literal inclusion of axioms is not required). If K is exactly the set of sentences derivable from F, then, if K taken as an axiom set does not prove a contradiction, the sentence “falsehood is not provable from the Craig presentation of F” is not in K. Thus, under these hypotheses, that sentence is not derivable from F. No assumption that every member of K is true in the standard natural numbers is required."}
translation: Target is the following proposition: For every set K of arithmetic sentences and every arithmetic theory F, assume that the axiom set F is recursively enumerable and that every theorem of IΣ₁ is a theorem of F (literal inclusion of axioms is not required). If K is exactly the set of sentences derivable from F, then, if K taken as an axiom set does not prove a contradiction, the sentence “falsehood is not provable from the Craig presentation of F” is not in K. Thus, under these hypotheses, that sentence is not derivable from F. No assumption that every member of K is true in the standard natural numbers is required.

divergences.description: Chalmers assumes soundness. The target requires only consistency, so it also covers consistent but unsound systems. This is the stated second-incompleteness generalization.

The target gives “sufficiently strong formal system” a concrete scope: recursively enumerable arithmetic theories proving every theorem of IΣ₁. It does not directly cover systems in other languages that interpret enough arithmetic.

The consistency sentence refers specifically to the Craig presentation of F. That presentation has exactly F’s theorems, so its consistency expresses the intended property, though the sentence need not be syntactically identical to one built from another presentation.

judgement.summary: The target captures item (c) in the claimed generality within its arithmetic setting. Since K is exactly F’s theorem set, consistency of K is equivalent to consistency of F, and nonmembership of the chosen consistency sentence in K is exactly its unprovability in F.
